To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the positively selected class I alleles of human MHC and the S-licus receptor kinase of the sporophyitic self-incompatibility (SSI) system of cruciferous plants are under physicochemically selective pressures to alter the polarity, volume, and charge of their encoded amino acids to various extents.

(a) at some sites, positively selected MHC proteins are under physiochemical selective pressures to change polarity, volume, and charge, and (b) at some sites in the positively selected SRK, polarity and volume are under selection.
the MHC class I alleles of known structure and SRK, a plant receptor kinase of unknown structure, are both under positive selective pressure.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification of sites in proteins that are under selective pressures to alter physicochemical properties, and the identification of the specific properties involved in these selective pressures.
developing and applying methods for identifying physicochemical selective pressure in the evolution of proteins.
the detection and characterization of site-specific selective pressures on amino acid sequences and with the identification of amino acid residues that may be important in ligand recognition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
both the MHC and SSI systems are under strong physicochemical selective pressure at some sites, but that this pressure is not the only one acting at the same sites.

the positively selected sites in the MHC and SSI are under selective pressures to change polarity, volume, and/or charge to some extent, and the MHC is under selective pressures to also change hydrophobicity.
both the MHC and SSI systems have undergone positive selection in their ligand-binding domains to maintain a balance between hydrophobicity and charge.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the class I alleles are under positive selection to alter polarity, and the SRK protein is under positive selection to modify polarity and volume.
the class I MHC and the SSI SRK are under physicochemically selective pressures that differ in nature and extent.
, in the MHC, positively selected amino acids are polar and/or charged, and that, in SRK, positively selected amino acid are polar and/or voluminous.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the physicochemical selective pressure model can be used to identify sites under positive selection in proteins of known structure and to predict sites under positive selection for proteins of unknown structure.

physicochemical selective pressure models are a useful tool to identify sites under positive selection, and to gain insight into the nature and extent to which these sites are under selection to change the physicochemical characteristics of the encoded amino acid.

the models of codon substitution that incorporate physico-chemical properties of amino acid sites are powerful tools for detecting site-specific selection pressures and identifying sites that may be functionally important.
